name: Dwang
catalog_citation: Essegbey, James. 2024. Catching and classifying fish among the Dwang. In Andrea Hollington, Alice Mitchell & Nico Nassenstein (eds.), Anthropological Linguistics: Perspectives from Africa (Culture and Language Use 23), 278-305. Amsterdam: John Benjamins. doi:10.1075/clu.23.11ess (OA, CC BY-NC-ND).
catalog_locator: footnote 3, p. 280; and section 2 (language background), p. 281
catalog_quote: I use broad transcriptions for the representations of Dwang words. Dwang is a tone language. Further research is required to determine the number of tonemes that the language possesses. For the purposes of this chapter, I represent phonetic (as opposed to phonemic) high tones alone with the acute accent. [...] In sum, Dwang, like all other Guang languages, is a tone language. It has vowel harmony and a noun class system with a paired set of prefixes, the choice of which is based on the tongue root position of the initial root vowel.

sources.citation: Olivencia, Julia, Adam McCollum & James Essegbey. 2022. Vowel patterns in Dwang: A phonetic and phonological analysis. Paper (abstract, 1 p.) at the 53rd Annual Conference on African Linguistics (ACAL 53), University of California San Diego (online), 7-9 April 2022.
sources.note: One-page conference abstract, self-described as 'to our knowledge, the first description of the language'. Content: eleven contrastive vowel qualities /i ɪ u ʊ e ɛ o ɔ a/ plus central /ə ɘ/ distinguished for ATR; /a/ alternates allophonically ([ɜ]/[ɐ]) before [+ATR] vowels; leftward ATR harmony with prefix alternations, partial harmony across compound boundaries; speculation on /l/~/r/ and harmony. Example words carry acute/grave tone diacritics (e.g. a-ʧɪ́ɪ́ 'women', sɔ̀ɔ̀ 'buy', kí-ɲí 'tooth') but the text makes no statement about tone or stress - tone marks in data only (wordlist-type evid…
